project_scope.note: Current canonical anchors are three Rhus taxa; poison-ivy comparison is taught as a safety/tie-breaker without requiring contact.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect a mature leaf node and rachis, then the flower/fruit cluster from a safe distance. Alternate exstipulate foliage may be trifoliolate or pinnate; a one-seeded drupe supports Anacardiaceae but is not unique. Compare leaflet attachment, winged rachis, fruit anatomy and inflorescence position. Never touch or crush suspected Toxicodendron.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Leaves may be trifoliolate or odd-pinnately compound; winged rachis and leaflet count are powerful local Rhus characters.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Small, usually 5-part flowers often with a nectar disk; local plants are woody and resinous.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Drupaceous and usually 1-seeded in the local learning set.
family_diagnostics.safety: Never use sap contact as an ID test. Toxicodendron resin can cause dermatitis.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Three leaflets do NOT diagnose poison ivy: Rhus aromatica and Toxicodendron can both be trifoliolate. Rhus copallinum/lanceolata has a conspicuously winged rachis. Confirm family and genus with safe-distance fruit clusters and flower/fruit architecture; avoid sap tests.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Sumac ID gets much easier when you stop treating 'three leaves' as poison ivy and instead read habit, rachis, leaflet texture and fruit.

steps.title: 1 · Three leaflets is not enough
steps.look_for: Exactly three leaflets on a low free-standing shrub rather than a climbing vine.
steps.why_it_matters: Rhus aromatica is the perfect antidote to the 'leaves of three' shortcut.

steps.title: 2 · Read the rachis
steps.look_for: Many narrow leaflets with conspicuous wing tissue along the rachis.
steps.why_it_matters: A winged rachis is one of the fastest local sumac characters.

steps.title: 3 · Notice evergreen architecture
steps.look_for: Only 5–9 thick glossy mostly entire leaflets on a large evergreen/semi-evergreen shrub.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows how broad Rhus foliage can be while retaining the family pattern.

steps.title: 4 · Confirm with the fruit
steps.look_for: Terminal clusters of red hairy one-seeded drupes.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit position/color/texture helps separate sumacs from poison ivy's paler drupes.

comparisons.title: Rhus aromatica vs poison ivy
comparisons.rule: Both may have 3 leaflets. Rhus aromatica is a low free-standing shrub with red hairy drupes; poison ivy commonly climbs/trails with aerial rootlets and pale whitish drupes.

comparisons.title: Anacardiaceae vs Sapindaceae
comparisons.rule: Resinous tissues and local red drupes favor Anacardiaceae; local Sapindaceae uses samaras, capsules or translucent drupes depending on genus.

comparisons.title: Rhus vs Toxicodendron: leaflets are not enough
comparisons.rule: Both can have three leaflets. Look for aerial rootlets where present and compare fruit clusters safely; T. rydbergii can be shrubby. Never touch unknown poison ivy.

comparisons.title: Rhus vs Sapindus (Sapindaceae)
comparisons.rule: Both may have alternate pinnate leaves and drupaceous fruits. Confirm fruit cutaway and flower/inflorescence architecture; drupes alone do not settle the family.

comparisons.title: Cotinus: feathers are not seeds
comparisons.rule: The long feathery parts of the smoke-tree fruiting panicle are elongated sterile pedicels, not plumed fruits. Inspect an actual attached fruit.

comparisons.title: Anacardiaceae vs Rutaceae
comparisons.rule: Check transmitted-light oil glands and fruit type (Rutaceae samaras/follicles/capsules vs Anacardiaceae drupes), not scent or leaf arrangement alone.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not crush, scratch, or handle unknown Anacardiaceae to test sap or odor.

family_confusion_polish.look_here_first: Leaf node and rachis first; reproductive fruit and inflorescence second. Do not rely on resin odor, red fruit, or three leaflets.

genus_routes.look_for: R. aromatica trifoliolate; R. copallinum/lanceolata pinnate with winged rachis; R. virens fewer thick evergreen leaflets; clustered one-seeded drupes. R. trilobata source names remain mapped to R. aromatica.
Trifoliolate leaves; T. radicans often climbing with aerial rootlets, T. rydbergii usually erect/shrubby; pale mature drupes in axillary clusters. Never handle for ID.
Simple rounded leaves; loose fruiting panicles with elongated feathery sterile pedicels (feathers are NOT plumose seeds).
Pinnate leaflets and small drupes; compare nodes and fruit rather than assuming a native Rhus.
Pinnate leaves and peppercorn-like drupes; distinguish from wing-rachis Rhus by rachis/fruit details.

family_comparisons.shared: Alternate pinnate leaves and one-seeded drupaceous fruits can overlap.
family_comparisons.separate: Inspect mature fruit and flower/inflorescence structure; do not use drupe alone. Other local Sapindaceae produce paired samaras or capsules.

family_comparisons.shared: Alternate compound leaves and small flowers with floral disks.
family_comparisons.separate: Backlight a leaf for pellucid oil-gland dots, then inspect Rutaceae samara/follicle/capsule versus Anacardiaceae drupe; gland absence in one photo is not proof.

family_comparisons.shared: Woody shrubs, sometimes three basal veins and drupes.
family_comparisons.separate: Look for stipules/thorns, 4–5-part disc flowers with stamens opposite petals and variable fruit; Anacardiaceae local members typically exstipulate.
A large hard nut inside a thick husk versus a smaller one-seeded drupe; compare cut mature fruits.

internal_confusions: Rhus aromatica vs Toxicodendron: both three leaflets; compare climbing aerial rootlets, fruit-cluster placement and mature drupe surface/color from a safe distance. T. rydbergii may be shrubby, so climbing habit alone is not proof.
Rhus copallinum/lanceolata vs Pistacia/Schinus: winged rachis versus generally unwinged; compare leaflets and mature fruit, not flower color.
Cotinus feather-like panicles: plumose structures are elongated sterile pedicels, not the fruit itself.
diagnostic_photo_roles: One matched trifoliolate Rhus aromatica and Toxicodendron leaf-node pair with petiole/leaflet/axil arrows; no touching Toxicodendron.
Close macro of Rhus copallinum/lanceolata winged rachis against Pistacia/Schinus unwinged rachis.
Safe-distance mature Rhus versus Toxicodendron fruit clusters, with axillary/terminal inflorescence labels; avoid color-only ID.
Cotinus fruiting panicle with arrows separating feathery sterile pedicels from actual fruit.
Mature Sapindus and Rhus drupe cutaways at matched scale, identifying pericarp and seed.
Backlit Rutaceae leaf oil glands versus Anacardiaceae leaflet and a matched fruit-type panel.
family_confusion_polish.image_policy: Use existing canonical Rhus species anchors first; new licensed macro acquisition and arrow overlays belong to Diagnostic Photo Polish. Preserve source rights and do not imply source photographs already include annotations.
family_confusion_polish.taxonomy_handoff: Preserve existing Rhus aromatica/trilobata synonym decisions and R. microphylla HOLD. Do not promote comparison taxa to target-zone native.
